pr.title: Reason about borrowed classes in CopyProp.
pr.description:
Fixes https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/141122

The current implementation of `CopyProp` avoids unifying two borrowed locals, as this would change the result of address comparison.

However, the implementation was inconsistent with the general algorithm, which identifies equivalence classes of locals and then replaces all locals by a single representative of their equivalence class.

This PR fixes it by forbidding the unification of two *classes* if any of those contain a borrowed local.

pr.author: cjgillot

analysis.summary: CopyProp's copy equivalence classes must be formed with borrowedness tracked at the class level, not patched only at replacement time. The historical implementation merged classes without regard to borrowed locals and then skipped replacement of individual borrowed locals during the visit; this could unify two distinct borrowed storages. The fix forbids merging two classes when both already contain a borrowed member, while still allowing a non-borrowed local to join a class that contains a borrowed local.
analysis.originalLogic: SsaLocals computes equivalence classes of locals linked by copy/move assignments, and CopyProp replaces all locals in a class by a single representative. The old Replacer carried `borrowed_locals` and, in `visit_local`, did `let new_local = self.copy_classes[*local]; if self.borrowed_locals.contains(*local) { return; }` before the context match. Its own comment stated: "We must not unify two locals that are borrowed. But this is fine if one is borrowed and the other is not. We chose to check the original local, and not the target. That way, if the original local is borrowed and the target is not, we do not pessimize the whole class." Crucially, `compute_copy_classes` itself had no borrowedness guard; it merged every copy edge, so class formation could still join two borrowed locals even though the per-use replacement guard kept the borrowed local's own name at its use sites.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Historically, CopyProp formed a copy equivalence class by merging the class of a copy destination with the class of its source without checking whether both classes contained borrowed locals. In the regression input, `_5 = copy _3` links two borrowed locals `_3` and `_5`, so the old class computation joined them (and `_4 = copy _5` joined `_4` to the same representative). Replacement-time skipping of borrowed locals did not undo that class merge: a non-borrowed member such as `_4` could still be rewritten to the shared class representative rather than being folded into `_5`'s separate class. The corrected transformation forbids the `_3`/`_5` merge, keeps `_5 = copy _3`, and allows non-borrowed `_4` to join `_5`'s class, so the call uses `_5` after `_4 = copy _5` is removed. The historical wrong rewrite is therefore the class-level merger of two borrowed locals (and consequent selection of a shared representative), not merely the old per-use guard.
analysis.trigger: A CopyProp input contains a copy/move assignment connecting two locals that are both recorded in `ssa.borrowed_locals()`, directly or because one side is already a class head whose class contains a borrowed member. Equivalently, the class being joined and the class of the source both satisfy `borrowed_classes.contains(...)`.
preconditions: CopyProp runs `SsaLocals::new` and `compute_copy_classes` on a MIR body.
At least two locals are borrowed and connected by a copy chain, e.g. `_5 = copy _3` where both `_3` and `_5` are borrowed.
A third local (e.g. `_4 = copy _5`) may copy one of the borrowed locals and later be used; it is not itself borrowed.
Address identity of the borrowed locals matters (references/raw pointers are taken), so conflating two borrowed storages can change observable behavior.
The merge guard must also propagate borrowedness correctly for the special `RETURN_PLACE` head-renaming path and for merges where only the destination is borrowed.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR functions with copy assignments, borrows (`&_x`, `core::ptr::addr_of!`) and possibly interleaved raw-pointer reads/writes, where two borrowed locals are linked through a copy chain and a non-borrowed local copies one of them. The supplied regression uses `#[custom_mir(dialect = "runtime")]` to make the MIR explicit.
pitfalls: Checking borrowedness only on the local currently being replaced is insufficient; the merge decision must be made when equivalence classes are formed.
The `borrowed_classes` bitset is keyed by class head. It must be updated when a non-borrowed local joins a borrowed class, and when the RETURN_PLACE class is renamed.

The rule is not 'never merge borrowed with non-borrowed'. It is: forbid the merge only when both classes contain a borrowed member. Merging a non-borrowed local into a borrowed class is explicitly allowed.

Do not conflate address-identity/borrowing restrictions with unrelated post-copy overwrite or storage-liveness conditions; the regression is about keeping two borrowed classes distinct, not about storage statements.
The invariant `borrowed_classes.contains(head) == any member of the class is borrowed` must hold for every class, as asserted in debug builds.
Removing the per-use borrowed-local guard is safe only after class formation itself prevents invalid merges.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a `tests/mir-opt/copy-prop/` custom-MIR test with `//@ test-mir-pass: CopyProp` and `// EMIT_MIR write_to_borrowed.main.CopyProp.diff`. In the MIR, borrow two locals connected by a copy (`_3 = const 'b'; _5 = copy _3; _6 = &_3; _4 = copy _5; ...; _6 = &_5; Call(_7 = dump_var(_4))`). Use `CHECK-NEXT` to assert `_5 = copy _3` survives, assert the call is `dump_var::<char>(copy _5)` and that `_4 = copy _5` is removed, and use `CHECK-NOT: {{_.*}} = {{_.*}};` in the relevant region to ensure the pass does not introduce an assignment to a borrowed local. The supplied diff shows the expected correction: `_4 = copy _5;` removed and the call rewritten from `copy _4` to `copy _5`, while `_3` and `_5` remain separate.

This PR fixes it by forbidding the unification of two *classes* if any of those contain a borrowed local.
